question: What is Kelvin–Voigt, exactly, as it applies to Gasper after the uniform-lp cut? How do the four lock τ map to E/η, phase, and discrete sa? Why not Maxwell or Zener?
coordinateSpaces: Content px. Discrete Voigt creep: x ← x+(x*−x)(1−e^{−dt/τ}). Exact solution of ẋ=(x*−x)/τ. τ in seconds. dt≈1/60 live, 1/120 on 120fps proof. No pascals. No mass in _lp (CoM k,c is the other organ). Stance sockets are x*, not paint.
physicalLaw: Kelvin–Voigt (spring ∥ dashpot): σ = E ε + η ε̇. Retardation time τ_R = η/E.
Creep under const σ: ε(t)=(σ/E)(1−e^{−t/τ}). Bounded. Approaches a shape. That is _lp toward the posed hull x*.
KV has no instantaneous elasticity (dashpot blocks a jump). KV has no stress relaxation under const ε (σ=Eε). Fine: we never hold strain and watch stress; we hold a target shape and creep to it.
After load removal a KV solid recovers fully: ε→0. Our analog is restHold: x* returns to the identity W and τ=0.42 creeps home. He does not puddle.
Maxwell (spring — dashpot): ė=σ̇/E+σ/η. Relaxation σ=σ0 e^{−t/τ} → 0. Creep unbounded. That is melt. Forbidden for a body that must hold a W.
Zener / SLS adds an extra spring (instant hop + creep + residual stress). Three constants. Forbidden (no E/η/ζ_KV sliders).
We store τ only. E and η are not recoverable from τ. If η is shared (one gel): E_a/E_b = τ_b/τ_a.
